title: What is your versioning format for deployments (Semantic Versioning), and how is the release/deployment process managed?
shortTitle: Versioning format for deployments (Semantic Versioning) and how the release/deployment process is managed

s1_definition.profdef: Semantic Versioning, abbreviated SemVer, is a versioning scheme of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where you increment MAJOR for backward-incompatible changes, MINOR for backward-compatible new features, and PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes. The release and deployment process wraps this version in a disciplined pipeline: a commit is tagged with a version, a continuous-integration pipeline builds and tests an immutable artifact stamped with that version, the artifact is promoted through environments (dev, staging, production) rather than rebuilt, and each promotion is gated by automated checks and, for production, approval. The version number is the single identity that ties a running pod back to an exact commit, a build log, and a changelog.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of how National Bank of India numbers its cheque books. A whole new cheque book design that old scanners cannot read is a big change (MAJOR). Adding a new field for UPI reference on the same design is a helpful new feature that old cheques still work alongside (MINOR). Fixing a typo in the fine print is a tiny fix (PATCH). The bank does not reprint cheques at each branch; it prints one official batch, stamps it with a serial, and ships that exact batch everywhere. SemVer is the serial on the software, and the release process is the controlled shipping of that one official batch.
s1_definition.oneliner: MAJOR means "I broke the contract," MINOR means "I added something safe," PATCH means "I fixed something quietly" — and you ship one versioned artifact everywhere, never rebuild per environment.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Semantic Versioning, abbreviated SemVer, is a versioning scheme of the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH where you increment MAJOR for backward-incompatible changes, MINOR for backward-compatible new features, and PATCH for backward-compatible bug fixes. The release and deployment process wraps this version in a disciplined pipeline: a commit is tagged with a version, a continuous-integration pipeline builds and tests an immutable artifact stamped with that version, the artifact is promoted through environments (dev, staging, production) rather than rebuilt, and each promotion is gated by automated checks and, for production, approval. The version number is the single identity that ties a running pod back to an exact commit, a build log, and a changelog.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of how National Bank of India numbers its cheque books. A whole new cheque book design that old scanners cannot read is a big change (MAJOR). Adding a new field for UPI reference on the same design is a helpful new feature that old cheques still work alongside (MINOR). Fixing a typo in the fine print is a tiny fix (PATCH). The bank does not reprint cheques at each branch; it prints one official batch, stamps it with a serial, and ships that exact batch everywhere. SemVer is the serial on the software, and the release process is the controlled shipping of that one official batch.

**One line to remember:** MAJOR means "I broke the contract," MINOR means "I added something safe," PATCH means "I fixed something quietly" — and you ship one versioned artifact everywhere, never rebuild per environment.

sections.s2_technical:
Semantic Versioning gives three numbers meaning so that anyone reading a version can predict the risk of upgrading. The version `2.4.1` means major version two, minor version four, patch one. If the Transfer Service publishes a library and bumps the major version to three, consumers know they must read the migration notes because something incompatible changed, such as a removed method or a changed response shape. If it bumps the minor version, consumers can upgrade safely to get new features without changing their code. If it bumps the patch version, it is a pure bug fix and upgrading is low risk. There is also a pre-release suffix such as `2.4.1-rc.1` for a release candidate and build metadata such as `+build.1842`.

A key discipline is that the version is assigned once and the artifact is immutable. You do not build the jar for staging and then build a different jar for production. You build `transfer-service-2.4.1.jar` exactly once, and that identical binary is promoted through environments. This matters enormously in banking because it means what you tested in staging is bit-for-bit what runs in production. Any difference between environments comes from configuration, which is injected at runtime, not from the code itself.

The release process is typically driven by a continuous-integration and continuous-delivery pipeline. When a pull request merges to the main branch, the pipeline runs: it compiles the code, runs unit and integration tests, performs static analysis and a security scan, and if everything passes, it builds the versioned artifact and a container image tagged with that version. The image is pushed to a registry. Then the pipeline promotes the image through environments. Promotion to development and staging is usually automatic. Promotion to production is gated by a manual approval, because moving money is involved, and often by additional checks such as a successful smoke test in staging.

The version in the build tool must stay consistent with the git tag. In Maven, the `<version>` in the pom is often derived from or matched to a git tag like `v2.4.1`. A common convention is that the main branch always carries a `-SNAPSHOT` version during development, and the act of releasing strips the snapshot, tags the commit, publishes the release artifact, and then bumps to the next snapshot. This is exactly what the Maven release process or tools like `jgitver` automate.

Deployments to Kubernetes reference the image by its immutable version tag, never by `latest`, because `latest` is ambiguous and makes rollbacks impossible to reason about. When a deployment goes wrong, rollback is simply re-pointing the deployment at the previous version tag, which is why the version is the anchor of the whole operational story.

The senior-level nuance is that the version is the join key across your entire toolchain. A running pod reports version `2.4.1` on its health endpoint; that string maps to a git tag, which maps to a commit, which maps to a pull request, which maps to a changelog entry and a build log. When an incident happens, that chain lets you answer "what exactly is running and what changed" in seconds. Teams enforce this with conventional commit messages that let tooling compute the correct version bump automatically: a commit marked as a breaking change forces a major bump, a feature forces a minor bump, and a fix forces a patch bump.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the Transfer Service is deployed continuously. The team needs a reliable way to decide what the next version number should be, based on the changes since the last release, and to record that decision in a changelog.

Problem 1 — A developer fixes a rounding bug in interest calculation. Another adds a new optional field to the transfer response. A third removes a deprecated endpoint that old clients no longer use. If the team guesses the next version by feel, they will sometimes under-signal a breaking change and surprise a downstream team. This is exactly the problem Semantic Versioning solves: the nature of the change determines the bump, removing guesswork.

Problem 2 — The team wants this to be automatic and auditable. If every commit follows a convention — a prefix saying whether it is a fix, a feature, or a breaking change — a tool can read the commits since the last tag and compute the correct next version deterministically. This is exactly how conventional-commit-driven release automation works.

Problem 3 — Auditors later ask "what changed between version 2.3.0 and 2.4.0 and why?" Without a generated changelog this is archaeology. With one, it is a single document. This is exactly why the release process generates a changelog from the same commits that drove the version bump.

To make this runnable, we will build a small program that models this decision. It will contain a `SemVer` class that parses and bumps a version, a `Commit` class with a type such as fix, feat, or breaking, a `ReleasePlanner` that reads a list of commits and computes the next version and a changelog, and a demo that feeds in a realistic set of commits for the Transfer Service and prints the computed next version and the changelog, exactly as a release pipeline would.
sections.s4a_structure:
Project structure:

```
release-tooling/
├── pom.xml
├── CHANGELOG.md                                  (generated artifact)
├── src/
│   ├── main/
│   │   ├── java/com/bank/release/
│   │   │   ├── ReleaseDemo.java                   (main class)
│   │   │   ├── model/
│   │   │   │   ├── SemVer.java                     (version value object)
│   │   │   │   └── Commit.java                     (conventional commit)
│   │   │   └── service/
│   │   │       └── ReleasePlanner.java             (computes next version)
│   │   └── resources/
│   │       └── application.yml
│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/release/
│           └── service/
│               └── ReleasePlannerTest.java
```

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
release:
  current-version: 2.3.0          # last released version read from the git tag
  snapshot-suffix: SNAPSHOT       # main branch carries -SNAPSHOT during dev
  changelog-path: CHANGELOG.md
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the release planner
java -jar target/release-tooling-1.0.0.jar

# In a real pipeline, the version then flows into the build and image tag:
mvn versions:set -DnewVersion=2.4.0
git tag v2.4.0
docker build -t registry.bank.local/transfer-service:2.4.0 .
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the current released version is 2.3.0, and there are three commits since that release — a fix to interest rounding, a new feature adding a UPI reference field, and a chore updating dependencies.

Step 1: The demo parses the string "2.3.0" into a SemVer object holding major two, minor three, patch zero.

Step 2: The ReleasePlanner scans the three commits to classify them. It finds no breaking change, one feature, and one fix. The chore is ignored for versioning.

Step 3: The planner applies the rule that the highest-impact change wins. There is no breaking change, so a major bump is ruled out. There is a feature, so a minor bump is selected. The fix would only have forced a patch bump, which the feature overrides.

Step 4: `bumpMinor` creates a new SemVer with the minor number increased from three to four and the patch reset to zero, producing 2.4.0. The original version object is untouched because SemVer is immutable.

Step 5: The planner builds a changelog. It groups commits by type, skipping empty sections. The Features section lists the UPI reference field, and the Fixes section lists the interest rounding correction. The chore and breaking sections are omitted because they are empty.

Step 6: The demo logs the transition from 2.3.0 to 2.4.0 and prints the changelog. In a real pipeline this version then becomes the Maven version, the git tag, and the container image tag, all identical, so the artifact has one unambiguous identity from source control to the running pod.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 1:20:11 AM com.bank.release.service.ReleasePlanner computeNextVersion
INFO: new feature detected -> MINOR bump
Oct 25, 2026 1:20:11 AM com.bank.release.ReleaseDemo main
INFO: next version: 2.3.0 -> 2.4.0
Oct 25, 2026 1:20:11 AM com.bank.release.ReleaseDemo main
INFO:
## 2.4.0

### Features
- add UPI reference field to transfer response

### Fixes
- correct rounding in interest calculation
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Developers push commits (conventional format)
    │  fix: interest rounding
    │  feat: UPI reference field
    │  chore: bump dependencies
    ▼
  Merge to main  ──→  CI/CD pipeline triggered
    │
    ▼
  ReleasePlanner.computeNextVersion(2.3.0, commits)
    │  breaking? no  →  feature? yes  →  MINOR bump
    ▼
  Next version = 2.4.0
    │
    ├──→ mvn versions:set 2.4.0  →  build transfer-service-2.4.0.jar (ONCE)
    ├──→ git tag v2.4.0
    ├──→ docker build ...:2.4.0  →  push to registry
    └──→ generate CHANGELOG.md
    │
    ▼
  Promote the SAME image 2.4.0 through environments
    dev (auto) ──→ staging (auto + smoke test) ──→ production (manual approval)
    │
    └─ rollback = re-point deployment to image tag 2.3.0
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Release Planner ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Value Object: SemVer is immutable; bump returns a NEW instance    │
  │     WHY: a version never mutates in place, safe to share           │
  │  Strategy-ish rule: highest-impact commit decides the bump         │
  │     WHY: deterministic, no human guesswork                         │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: SemVer models a version; ReleasePlanner decides bumps          │
  │  O: new commit type? extend the enum + one rule, nothing breaks    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────────────┐
  │   SemVer (immutable)  │         │   ReleasePlanner        │
  │──────────────────────│         │─────────────────────────│
  │ - major:int          │◀────────│ + computeNextVersion()  │
  │ - minor:int          │ returns │ + buildChangelog()      │
  │ - patch:int          │         │ - appendSection()       │
  │ + bumpMajor/Minor/... │        └───────────┬─────────────┘
  └──────────────────────┘                     │ reads List<Commit>
                                                ▼
                                   ┌─────────────────────────┐
                                   │   Commit                │
                                   │ + Type {FIX,FEAT,        │
                                   │   BREAKING,CHORE}        │
                                   │ + message:String        │
                                   └─────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: version lifecycle on main ─────────────
  [2.3.0 released] → [2.4.0-SNAPSHOT dev] → release → [2.4.0 tagged]
        → [2.5.0-SNAPSHOT dev] ...

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. ReleaseDemo.main()
  2.   → SemVer.parse("2.3.0")
  3.   → ReleasePlanner.computeNextVersion(current, commits)
  4.       → scan commits: breaking? feature? fix?
  5.       → SemVer.bumpMinor() → 2.4.0
  6.   → ReleasePlanner.buildChangelog(2.4.0, commits)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
My versioning format is Semantic Versioning, which is three numbers in the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and each position carries a clear contract. I increment the major number for any backward-incompatible change, such as removing an endpoint or changing a response shape, because that tells every consumer they must read the migration notes before upgrading. I increment the minor number for backward-compatible new features, so a consumer can upgrade safely to gain functionality without changing their own code. And I increment the patch number for backward-compatible bug fixes, which are the lowest-risk upgrades. This discipline means a version number alone communicates the risk of adopting a new release, which is exactly what downstream teams and auditors need.

The release process is built around the principle that the version is assigned once and the artifact is immutable. When a pull request merges to the main branch, the pipeline runs tests, static analysis, and a security scan, then builds the versioned jar and container image exactly once and pushes the image to a registry tagged with that version. That identical image is then promoted through environments — automatically to development and staging, and to production only after a smoke test passes and a human approves, because this is a bank and the service moves money. I never deploy by the latest tag, always by the explicit version, because that makes rollback trivial: I simply re-point the deployment at the previous version tag.

To make the version bump deterministic rather than a matter of opinion, I use conventional commit messages. A commit marked as a breaking change forces a major bump, a feature forces a minor bump, and a fix forces a patch bump, and the highest-impact commit since the last release wins. A tool reads those commits and computes both the next version and a grouped changelog automatically, which means the changelog is never out of date and the auditors always have a clear record of what changed between any two releases and why.

At National Bank of India, this paid off directly. On one release of the Transfer Service we had a rounding fix and a new optional UPI reference field, so the tooling computed a minor bump from 2.3.0 to 2.4.0, generated the changelog, built one image tagged 2.4.0, and promoted that exact image to production after approval. When a minor issue surfaced an hour later, rolling back was a single command re-pointing the deployment at image tag 2.3.0, and because the artifact was immutable we knew precisely what we were reverting to. The version number was the thread that tied the running pod back to the commit, the pull request, and the changelog, which is what makes incident response fast and auditable.
